lesson.title: Kepler's laws

steps.headline: Each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

lead.text: An ellipse is a stretched circle. Half its longest diameter is the semi-major axis, a. The eccentricity, e, says how stretched it is: 0 is a circle. The closest point to the Sun is perihelion and the farthest is aphelion.
The Sun sits a distance a × e from the centre of the ellipse, towards one end. Earth's e is 0.017, so its distance from the Sun changes by only about 3%.

reveal.text: Perihelion is a − a × e, which is a(1 − e). Whatever you guessed, the stretch e pulls the closest point in from a by the fraction e.

steps.headline: Find the aphelion distance when a = 3 AU and e = 0.5.

workedSteps.text: The far end is the centre-to-Sun gap, a × e, beyond a.

steps.headline: A planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at perihelion.

lead.text: This is Kepler's second law. The line from Sun to planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun that line is short, so the planet must cover a longer arc in the same time. It speeds up.
At the two ends of the long axis, the speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances from the Sun.

reveal.text: The planet is four times faster at perihelion than at aphelion. Equal areas in equal times forces the speed to change this much.

lead.text: Kepler's third law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. With P in years and a in AU around the Sun, P² = a³. The period depends only on a, not on e.

reveal.text: P² = 64, so P = 8: a bigger orbit takes much longer than its size alone suggests, because the planet also moves slower.

lead.text: Around a star of M solar masses the law becomes P² = a³ ÷ M. A stronger pull needs a faster orbit to keep from falling inward.

reveal.text: A heavier star shortens the period: the same orbit size is covered more quickly because the pull is stronger.

lesson.orientation: Describe an orbit by its size and shape, and link its period to its semi-major axis.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A comet's orbit is a long oval. The Sun sits inside it, on the line through the oval's two ends. At its closest the comet is 1 AU from the Sun, and at its farthest 9 AU.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find an orbit's closest and farthest points and use its size to work out its period.

recap.keyIdea: A planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, fastest at perihelion. Its period in years and semi-major axis in AU satisfy P² = a³.

blocks.text: You found that an orbit running from 1 AU to 9 AU has a long axis of 10 AU, and that an asteroid with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6 moves four times faster at perihelion. A 4 AU orbit takes 8 years.

recap.nextHook: Kepler described the orbits without explaining them. What force makes a planet follow them?

questions.prompt: An asteroid's orbit has semi-major axis 2 AU and eccentricity 0.6. How close does it come to the Sun, in AU?
hints: The Sun sits at a focus, a × e from the centre.
Perihelion distance is a(1 − e).
Calculate 2 × (1 − 0.6).
questions.onCorrect: 0.8 AU. The Sun sits a × e from the centre, so perihelion is a(1 − e).

misconceptions.feedback: That is a × e, the gap between the Sun and the centre. Closest approach is measured from the Sun, so take that gap off a.
That is the far end. The closest point lies on the near side of the Sun.

questions.prompt: For the orbit with a = 2 AU and e = 0.6, the speed at perihelion divided by the speed at aphelion equals the aphelion distance divided by the perihelion distance. Find this ratio.
hints: Aphelion is a(1 + e) and perihelion is a(1 − e).
Work out both distances.
Divide 3.2 by 0.8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Aphelion 3.2 AU ÷ perihelion 0.8 AU = 4. The asteroid moves four times faster at its closest point.

questions.onCorrect: 4. The speeds are in the inverse ratio of the distances, so the closer end is faster.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. The planet is faster at the closer end.
That is the aphelion distance, not a ratio of the two distances.

questions.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with semi-major axis 4 AU. Using P² = a³ (P in years, a in AU), find its period in years.
hints: Cube the semi-major axis.
That gives P².
Take the square root of 64.
questions.onCorrect: 8 years. Cube a to get P², then take the square root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². The law gives the square of the period, so take the square root.
That is the square root of a. The law cubes a first.

questions.prompt: A planet orbits a star of 4 solar masses with a = 1 AU. Using P² = a³/M, find its period in years.
hints: Divide a³ by the star's mass in solar masses.
1 cubed is 1.
Take the square root of a quarter.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 years. A heavier star divides P² by M, so the period shrinks.

misconceptions.feedback: That is P². Take the square root to get the period.
That is the period around a Sun-like star. A heavier star pulls harder and shortens it.

questions.prompt: Jupiter's orbital period is 11.86 years. Using P² = a³, find its semi-major axis in AU, to two decimal places.
hints: Square the period to get a³.
11.86² is about 140.7.
Take the cube root of that.
questions.onCorrect: 5.20 AU. Square the period to get a³, then take the cube root.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a³. Take the cube root to find a.
That is the square root of the period. P² = a³ makes a the cube root of P².

questions.prompt: What name is given to the point of a planet's orbit closest to the Sun?
hints: It begins with the Greek prefix for 'near'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Perihelion, from Greek peri (near) and helios (Sun). The farthest point is aphelion.

questions.onCorrect: Perihelion: peri means near and helios means Sun.

misconceptions.feedback: Aphelion is the farthest point. The closest point has the prefix that means near.

questions.prompt: How long is the oval along its longest direction, in AU?
hints: Picture the long line through the two ends, with the Sun on it.
The comet's closest and farthest points are the two ends.
Add the two distances.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two ends are 1 AU and 9 AU from the Sun, on either side of it: 1 + 9 = 10 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 10 AU. The long axis is the closest and farthest distances added together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the difference of the distances. The Sun lies between the ends, so the two distances add.
That is only the far end. The long axis also includes the near side.

questions.prompt: What is the eccentricity of a perfect circle?
hints: Eccentricity measures how stretched the ellipse is.
questions.onCorrect: A circle is not stretched at all, so e is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: An eccentricity near 1 means a long, thin ellipse, the opposite of a circle.
A half-way value is a fairly stretched ellipse, not a circle.

hints: Where is the Sun, compared with the centre of the ellipse?

acceptedIdeas: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.

choices.label: The Sun is off-centre by a × e, so the far end is a + a × e from it.
Because e is always larger than 1.
Because aphelion is measured from the planet.

questions.onCorrect: The Sun is a × e from the centre, so the far end is that much farther than a.

misconceptions.feedback: e is between 0 and 1 for an ellipse. The 1 + e comes from the Sun's off-centre position.
Both distances are measured from the Sun. The planet is at the point being measured.

questions.prompt: Where does a planet move slowest?
hints: Where is the line from the Sun to the planet longest?

choices.label: It moves at the same speed everywhere

questions.onCorrect: A long line sweeps the same area with a short arc, so the planet is slowest at aphelion.

misconceptions.feedback: At perihelion the line is shortest, so the planet moves fastest.
Equal areas in equal times needs the speed to change as the distance does.

questions.prompt: A comet has perihelion 0.5 AU and aphelion 7.5 AU. Find its semi-major axis, in AU.
hints: The long axis runs from the near end to the far end through the Sun.
Add the two distances to get the long axis.
a is half the long axis.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The long axis is 0.5 + 7.5 = 8 AU, and a is half of it: 4 AU.

questions.onCorrect: 4 AU. The semi-major axis is half the sum of the closest and farthest distances.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole long axis. The semi-major axis is half of it.
That is the difference of the two distances. The long axis is their sum.
